questions.question: The header, cart page and checkout summary must show the same cart quantities immediately. Which owner fits this client-side data?
options: One reducer-backed cart owner shared through context, with all three views reading it.
Three independent useState copies that each save to local storage.
A separate query key for each header render.
The checkout form owns the cart, and the header reads the form DOM.
feedback: Correct. The shared reducer gives coordinated transitions and one source for the rendered quantities. Persistence may be added separately.
Independent copies can disagree within the same browser. Writing storage does not automatically synchronize those React state values.
Query identity describes server data requests, not an arbitrary render or this client-owned cart.
The cart is shared application state. A form DOM read would couple the header to one screen and miss its own updates.

questions.question: A helper asserts an unknown JSON body as EventItem. Which change establishes runtime confidence in the response shape?
options: Annotate a second variable with EventItem.
Run the body through the event schema and handle a failed parse.
Put EventItem in the query key.
Use a longer staleTime.
feedback: A type annotation does not inspect values received at runtime.
Correct. The schema checks the actual value. The helper must reject or otherwise handle the failed parse; TypeScript then follows the checked result.
The key identifies a cached result. It does not validate the response body.
Freshness policy changes cache reuse, not response validation.
questions.revisit: Zod Schemas & Type Inference; Server State & Query Setup (the checked helper)

questions.question: The same list endpoint receives category=food on page1 and category=food on page2. How should the query keys reflect those requests?
options: Use one constant events key because the endpoint path is the same.
Include only the category; pagination is visual state.
Include the normalized category, page and every other value that changes the requested result.
Use a random key every time to guarantee a new request.
feedback: The results differ even though the endpoint path is shared. One key would mix their cache identity.
The page changes which records the server returns, so it belongs in the identity too.
Correct. The key and query function must agree on the complete request inputs. Equivalent normalized values should identify the same result.
Random keys prevent meaningful reuse and can grow the cache with unrelated entries.

questions.question: A title PATCH returns the complete accepted event. That title can change list search matches and page order. Which update path matches the example?
options: Replace the exact detail entry with the accepted record, then invalidate the event-list prefix.
Change only the visible card text and leave cached list totals untouched.
Invalidate only the detail key and assume every list updates automatically.
Clear all React state and reload the entire document after every save.
feedback: Correct. The detail can use the checked full response. List invalidation lets the server recalculate membership, ordering and totals for matching queries.
Changing a label does not repair search membership, pagination or totals.
The detail and lists have separate keys. Invalidating the detail does not automatically invalidate those list entries.
A document reload discards useful state and avoids the intended cache update rather than implementing it.

questions.question: An optimistic publication changes a cached event from draft to published. The server rejects it. What must the recovery path accomplish?
options: Hide the error because the optimistic badge already changed.
Restore the previously captured record to the affected entry and keep useful failure feedback.
Keep the predicted record and retry forever.
Mutate the snapshot object in place before restoring it.
feedback: The user would see a state the server did not accept, with no explanation.
Correct. The snapshot preserves the earlier accepted display; immutable prediction keeps that snapshot usable for restoration.
Unbounded retries do not make a rejected business rule valid and prolong an incorrect display.
Mutating the snapshot destroys the earlier value needed for recovery.

questions.question: The loader and EventDetail use the same client and eventOptions key. The title form already uses a mutation that updates detail data and invalidates lists. What should the routed screen do?
options: Copy the loader result into a new useState owner, then keep both copies synchronized manually.
Create a new QueryClient each time the detail component renders.
Add a route action that submits the same title PATCH again after the mutation.
Subscribe through useQuery to the existing entry and retain the existing mutation-owned write path.
feedback: A duplicate state owner can become stale after cache updates and adds unnecessary synchronization.
A new client would fragment or repeatedly reset the cache and lose shared reuse.
Submitting the same write twice creates duplicate side effects and unclear error/refresh ownership.
Correct. The loader prepares the cached record, the query observer subscribes, and the mutation keeps responsibility for that feature's writes and cache updates.
